learning by doing is important, but vintage is more important, and that selection is not important.

the impact of experience on performance, but we are also concerned with the impact on performance of the fact that some teachers have been teaching for longer than others, and we are also concerned about the impact on performance that is related to the selection of individuals into the teaching profession.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between teaching performance and experience depends on the type of experience that is being measured.
the impact of teaching experience on teaching performance is positive, but that the magnitude of this impact is overestimated when the impact of vintage is not accounted for.
the relationship between experience, learning and performance in the teaching profession is positive, but that the impact of the learning process on performance is not as strong as is often believed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impact of experience on teaching performance is underestimated in cross-sections.

, while the relationship between teaching performance and years of teaching experience may be weak, there is a strong relationship between the two if the years of experience reflect the teacher’s ability to learn from teaching experience.
learning by doing and selection are the two most relevant phenomena that influence the relationship between teaching performance and experience.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between teaching performance and years of teaching experience is not necessarily linear, and that the relationship is influenced by the way experience is measured.
the puzzling relationship between experience and teaching performance observed in a sample of teachers is due in part to vintage and selection effects.
the relationship between experience, learning by doing, and performance is likely to be underestimated when cross-sectional data on experience are used.
